newsitem.title: USA: U.S., North Korea to search for missing troops.
newsitem.headline: U.S., North Korea to search for missing troops.

text.p: The United States and North Korea have agreed to conduct three new searches for remains of U.S. troops missing in the North since the Korean War and to examine archives in Pyongyang for information on missing Americans, the Pentagon said on Thursday.

But there was no immediate agreement from the North on a request by the United States to interview several U.S. military defectors believed to be living in North Korea since the 1960s, the Defence Department said.
The announcement of the agreement, sealed on Wednesday, followed five days of talks between U.S. and North Korean officials in New York last week.
Those talks ended on Friday night in what then appeared to be no progress in the effort to account for some 8,100 U.S. troops still missing in the North since the 1950-53 war.

Larry Greer, a spokesman for the Pentagon office in charge of missing American troops, said he expected the first of the three searches to begin within a month and that Washington had agreed to pay Pyongyang $105,500 in expenses for each joint excavation.
The one-page agreement also sets up "in principle" a search of archives in the Fatherland Liberation War Museum in Pyongyang for information on missing Americans.
Greer did not say where the excavations for remains would take place, but said the United States wanted to search sites including single aircraft crashes and perhaps mass burial sites of U.S. troops.
"We're prepared to do the first one very, very soon, within the month. And the farthest that we can go out is perhaps into the fall, when the ground freezes," he told reporters.
"The types of sites we are looking for are individual airplane crashes as well as mass burial sites."
Washington also wants to find out the fate of six American troops who defected to the North in the 1960s, four of whom are believed to be still alive.
The Pentagon said there was no agreement on the U.S. request to talk to these Americans but that negotiations would continue on that issue.

"We think four of the six who defected are still alive. We have seen them, as some of you know, in propaganda publications, magazines, films, what not, and as far we know, they are still alive," Greer told reporters.
Last week's negotiations were the fourth in the series that began in 1996. Talks one year ago resulted in a joint operation in North Korea that led to the return of an American soldier's remains.
But a second excavation scheduled for the fall of 1996 fell through after a North Korean submarine loaded with commandos ran aground last September off South Korea.
